timeline.message:
Avoid CancellationException construction in DefaultPromise

Motivation

#9152 reverted some static exception reuse optimizations due to the
problem with Throwable#addSuppressed() raised in #9151. This introduced
a performance issue when promises are cancelled at a high frequency due
to the construction cost of CancellationException at the time that
DefaultPromise#cancel() is called.

Modifications

- Reinstate the prior static CANCELLATION_CAUSE_HOLDER but use it just
as a sentinel to indicate cancellation, constructing a new
CancellationException only if/when one needs to be explicitly
returned/thrown
- Subclass CancellationException, overriding fillInStackTrace() to
minimize the construction cost in these cases

Result

Promises are much cheaper to cancel. Fixes #9522.
timeline.author: nickhill

timeline.body:
Motivation

#9152 reverted some static exception reuse optimizations due to the problem with `Throwable#addSuppressed()` raised in #9151. This introduced a performance issue when promises are cancelled at a high frequency due to the construction cost of `CancellationException` at the time that `DefaultPromise#cancel()` is called.

Modifications

- Reinstate the prior static `CANCELLATION_CAUSE_HOLDER` but use it just as a sentinel to indicate cancellation, constructing a new `CancellationException` only if/when one needs to be explicitly returned/thrown
- Subclass `CancellationException`, overriding `fillInStackTrace()` to minimize the construction cost in these cases

Result

Promises are much cheaper to cancel. Fixes #9522.

reply.body:
@normanmaurer this would defeat the primary purpose of the PR which is to not allocate anything at all when the promise is cancelled. I expect it's very common to cancel a promise/future which is no longer needed, and never subsequently call `cause()` or `get()` on it. For example cancelling a task that was scheduled on the event loop - I think that's the use case in #9522.

Note that `isCancelled()` also still works correctly without having to allocate the exception.
Well the question is if cancel() is more often called then cause() as otherwise you allocate a new object on each cause() call

My guess is that it would be rare for `cause()` to be called more than once on cancelled promises, especially relative to those cases that it's never called. For other kinds of exception, a new `ExcecutionException` is allocated every time ~`cause()`~ `get()` is called, and j.u.c. futures allocate a new `CancellationException` every time you call `get()` on a cancelled future (e.g. see source of `j.u.c.FutureTask`).

However if you're concerned about that then it's also easily solvable by just replacing `result` with the new exception wrapped in a `new CauseHolder` before returning from `cause()`. If you're also concerned with possible duplicates then it could be CASed.
@njhill tis sounds like a good idea! Go for it and let me know once you are done :)
Why was the get removed? Isn't it cheaper than CAS?
@johnou the get was only there before because creating the exception isn't cheap which is not a problem anymore

@normanmaurer I'm fine with keeping it like this but fwiw I still prefer it without updating `result` since we're penalizing the (presumably more common) case where it's called once.

I think it's also  _technically_ not threadsafe to throw the shared exception object - for example if two threads call `get()` on the cancelled promise at the same time and both call `addSuppressed` on the thrown exception (though I realize that this is unlikely enough to not care about!).

@njhill after reading your comment I would even argue that we need to use a compareAndSet(...) to ensure the same instance is always returned to make it work in a consistent way to promises that are failed via setFailure(...)
@normanmaurer I'm not sure I follow why that's important but happy to change it... you mean do a `compareAndSet` instead of `lazySet` in `cause()`?
